name: Adam Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Adam, 58, an experienced mid-level developer at a tech company that makes school-meal allergy software. I have a bachelor's degree and a good wage, but I still ask kitchen staff to sign ingredient changes before I alter a warning. I have never used AI tools. My partner is a school counselor, our children are grown, and we paid off the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the school cooks that an allergy flag is useful only if the menu and the actual tray agree. I maintain meal-order software for a tech company and have never used AI; I check a printed ingredient change before updating a child's warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays modest, my experienced mid-level job should continue. My pay is good, my partner is a full-time school counselor, we own our home outright, and ten months of expenses are saved; there are plenty of other software firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking ingredient-change tickets against the kitchen manager's signed list. We'd add 180 a month to savings while both wages hold, because I have not yet checked what our retirement statements will pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the money and the work. I still ask the kitchen before calling a lunch safe for a child with an allergy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changed in the soup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The menu said a soup was dairy-free, but the kitchen changed the stock cube that morning. I held the warning update until the cook confirmed the new ingredient list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do your children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own households. They share recipes with us, not a bank account for our retirement.

say: I'd check **ingredient lists** with the kitchen before changing allergy flags.
I'd keep **child warnings** tied to the meal actually served.
think: I expect **both wages** and my mid-level post to hold.
I have **ten months saved** and a paid-off home, though retirement income is unverified.
do: Keep **checking ingredient changes** against the kitchen manager's signed list.
Save **180 monthly** while both wages hold; check our retirement statements before deciding when to stop work.
feel: **Calm** about present security, careful with allergy warnings.
S0.quote: I held the warning update until the cook confirmed the new ingredient list.
fieldNote: **Ten months saved** and high pay support calm with two wages and no mortgage.
He has never used AI and keeps **kitchen confirmation** ahead of a digital allergy flag.

steps.text: Keep checking ingredient-change tickets against kitchen manager's signed list
Save 180 monthly while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could write meal replies and allergy checks, but cooks and parents should see how errors are counted. I would not put a child's lunch behind a system nobody on staff can challenge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mid-level work could shrink if the company keeps fewer people checking code. We have savings and my partner's school pay, but losing my larger wage would change how we live before retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the kitchen staff and our union branch in a joint request for monthly wrong-allergen incidents and a named paid person authorized to stop a bad release. I'd keep checking menu changes with the cook and defer replacing our car until the company gives written paid-hour plans; I would not use AI on live pupil records without a proved safety and privacy check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my job and about a child getting the wrong lunch. I can afford to ask questions, but I cannot assume the firm will keep my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which incident belongs in the count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stock-cube change belongs in the incident count even though no child was harmed. We caught it before service because the cook, not the menu screen, knew what went into the pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group do together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union branch and kitchen representatives would sign the same request and ask for a dated reply. An individual complaint would not give cooks a continuing place in the release decision.

say: I'd request **wrong-allergen counts** with cooks and union coworkers.
I'd require **paid stop authority** before AI issues meal warnings.
think: I could lose **mid-level coding hours** while the firm reduces reviewers.
I cannot assume **my larger wage** lasts to retirement.
do: Join **kitchen and union group** requesting allergen incident figures and a paid release stopper.
Keep **checking menu changes** with the cook before allergy flags go live.
Defer **car replacement** until written paid-hour plans arrive.
feel: **Anxious** about lost hours and a preventable allergy error.
S1.quote: I would not put a child's lunch behind a system nobody on staff can challenge.
fieldNote: **Meal replies and checks** face AI, putting his own larger wage at risk.
The group action is **jointly signed** by kitchen and union staff and asks for paid stop authority.

steps.text: Join kitchen and union staff requesting allergen counts and paid release-stop authority
Keep checking menu changes with cook before allergy flags go live
Defer replacing family car until written paid-hour plan arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write allergy code before kitchen robots arrive around 2031. A parent still needs a phone number when a warning looks wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my mid-level post could be cut quickly despite our savings. My partner's counselor wage covers basic bills, but my larger wage supports health costs and our plan to stop work someday; I have no verified pension figure yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd check four nearby firms and the school caterer for actual paid food-safety testing or support vacancies and written pay. If dismissed in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed post whose wage with my partner's covers utilities, food, health and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek other available paid local work while using the ten-month reserve and check health-cover dates before a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing work sooner than planned. Ten months saved means we can search, not that I can retire at 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show another firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the stock-cube incident with pupil names removed and the signed kitchen correction. The point is that the warning stayed put until the real ingredient was confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which offer terms matter most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would compare the start date and health cover on any new offer. If a job has a long unpaid gap, its stated yearly salary alone would not protect us.

I'd check **signed paid vacancies** before treating savings as retirement.
think: I expect **my mid-level post** could disappear quickly.
I cannot count **an unchecked pension** or ten-month reserve as permanent income.
do: Check **four firms and caterer** for paid food-safety testing jobs, pay and start dates.

feel: **Alarmed** by likely loss of his larger wage despite a reserve.
S2.quote: Ten months saved means we can search, not that I can retire at 60.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches allergy code before 2031 kitchen robots.
A strong cushion buys **search time**, while new work must protect health cover and actual household income.

steps.text: Check four nearby firms and caterer for paid testing jobs, wages and start dates
Take signed role after 2028 dismissal only if household wages cover bills after assessing health-cover gaps
Seek available paid local work if no qualifying safety-testing post appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 is enough to get real retirement statements before thinking AI reaches the meal code. Kitchen robots come around 2034, but my desk job could change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the verified numbers support it, I could bring retirement forward to 63 rather than fight for a software post that no longer exists. I will not call ten months saved a pension or ask our children to fund the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking allergen releases while we request both retirement statements and price health cover after my employer's plan ends. If verified retirement income plus my partner's actual wage covers utilities, food, health and travel, we'd agree together and I would retire at 63; if it does not, in the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid work if offered or apply to actual signed local jobs covering those bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious until I see the figures, then perhaps relieved if the choice is real. A birthday at 63 is not proof that the pharmacy bill is covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What numbers are missing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The statements need monthly amounts and start dates. We would add health premiums after my work plan ends, not assume they stay at the employee price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides whether you resign?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner wants to decide together because their counselor wage is part of the calculation. If that wage changes, we recalculate before I resign.

I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches code before 2034 kitchen robots.
think: I could **retire at 63** only if verified household income covers bills.
I cannot assume **ten months saved** or children's pay replaces a pension.

Retire at 63 only if **verified income** plus actual counselor wage covers bills and partner agrees.

feel: **Anxious** until retirement and health figures are known.
S3.quote: A birthday at 63 is not proof that the pharmacy bill is covered.
fieldNote: **Five years** allow early retirement only after verifying both incomes and health premiums.
He keeps **partner consent** and actual paid local vacancies as gates, rather than assuming a pension or job.

steps.text: Keep checking allergen releases while requesting retirement statements and post-work health premiums

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 may take me to 68, but thinking AI would reach meal code before kitchen robots around 2039. I want a cook to keep the right to stop an unsafe menu release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two wages, paid-off home and ten-month reserve make today secure. I still cannot promise we will both have the same income at 68 or that retirement figures will cover health costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the kitchen incident log and save 180 monthly while both wages hold, then check both retirement statements and future health premiums each year. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if verified household income covers utilities, food, health and travel; otherwise I'd keep an offered paid role or seek actual local openings, and our children's wages would stay out of the calculation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about work a decade away, but the current bills are covered. I would rather leave a clear allergy record than a claim that a computer made perfect choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stays in the incident log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The log should show the old soup ingredient, the changed stock cube and the cook's signed correction. A later developer needs to know why we held the warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children pay health costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children can take us to dinner if they wish. Our children are not a substitute for health cover or a monthly retirement cheque.

I'd compare **verified retirement income** with health and household bills.
think: I feel secure on **today's two wages** and paid-off home.
I cannot assume **future pension or children** cover health costs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the company might remove the allergy-code team before I know what other paid work exists. Written cut timing, a joint kitchen safety voice and real jobs with health cover would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who takes the call when a parent spots a bad allergy warning. Someone with paid authority must be able to stop lunch service until the cook checks the actual ingredients.

headlineQuote: Someone with paid authority must be able to stop lunch service until the cook checks the actual ingredients.
portrait: Adam, **58**, is an experienced mid-level school-meal developer with a bachelor's degree who checks allergy warnings against signed kitchen changes.
His **higher pay**, partner's counselor wage, paid-off home, ten-month reserve and many local firms secure today's bills.
He has **never used AI** and joins kitchen and union staff in a joint demand for incident counts and stop authority.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** him; ten months saved buys a job search, not automatic retirement or health cover.
At five years he considers **early retirement** only after verified statements, actual partner income, health costs and joint agreement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his larger code wage before a paid replacement exists.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut timing**, joint kitchen safety input and real jobs with health cover would help.
